Deal
dēl
v. (to distribute or apportion; to act toward a person; rendering Hebrew gamal, bagad, Greek merizo)
From Saxon dælan, to divide or distribute. The word keeps both halves in Scripture: to deal is to hand out bread, and to deal is to conduct oneself toward another — bountifully, or treacherously.

Biblical Definition

Deal in the Authorized Version carries two senses that Scripture keeps close together: to distribute a thing, and to conduct oneself toward a person. Isaiah puts the first at the head of the fast God chooses: “Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?” (Isaiah 58:7). The bread is thy bread, dealt out by the hand that owns it, and the last clause forbids the convenient blindness that gives to strangers while ignoring kin. The second sense is covenantal and can be violated: “Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us? why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother, by profaning the covenant of our fathers?” (Malachi 2:10). Treachery between brothers is treated as a profaning of the covenant, not merely as a private wrong. Against both stands the way God deals with His own, which is stated first negatively — “He hath not dealt with us after our sins; nor rewarded us according to our iniquities” (Psalm 103:10) — and then positively, as the ground of song: “I will sing unto the LORD, because he hath dealt bountifully with me” (Psalm 13:6).

Webster 1828 Definition

To divide; to distribute; to give out in portions; also, to conduct oneself toward another, well or ill. Scripture commands dealing bread to the hungry, forbids dealing treacherously with a brother, and grounds praise in God's bountiful dealing with sinners.

expand to see more

DEAL, v.t. [Sax. dælan, to divide.] To divide; to part; to separate; hence, to divide in portions; to distribute; as, to deal out bread to the poor.

2. To scatter; to throw about; as, to deal blows among the enemy.

3. To distribute the cards of a pack to the players.

DEAL, v.i. To traffick; to trade; to negotiate; as, to deal in silks.

2. To act between man and man; to intervene; to behave well or ill; as, to deal justly with all men.

DEAL, n. A part or portion; a distribution; also, an indefinite quantity or degree; as, a great deal of time.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 58:7 — "Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?"

Malachi 2:10 — "Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us? why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother, by profaning the covenant of our fathers?"

Psalm 103:10 — "He hath not dealt with us after our sins; nor rewarded us according to our iniquities."

Psalm 13:6 — "I will sing unto the LORD, because he hath dealt bountifully with me."

Modern Corruption

Isaiah 58 has been enlisted for a politics of redistribution, so that the personal duty of dealing one's own bread to the hungry is transferred to the state and the man himself is excused from the fast God chose.

expand to see more

Isaiah 58:7 is among the most quoted texts in progressive religion, and the quotation nearly always drops the possessive. The prophet says thy bread, and the acts he lists are all personal and costly: bringing the poor that are cast out into thy house, covering the naked thou seest, refusing to hide from thine own flesh. Transfer the duty to an agency and every element of the fast disappears — the bread is no longer the giver's, the poor man never enters his house, and the giver never sees the naked he covers. The chapter is a rebuke of religious performance, and administering a policy is a performance available to a man whose own door stays shut. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: names the redistributive reading of Isaiah 58 in order to rebut it

The opposite corruption seizes on that argument to evade the text altogether, treating Isaiah 58 as ancient ceremony and mercy to the poor as optional. Scripture forecloses that too. The fast God chooses is defined by these acts, Malachi ties dealing treacherously with a brother to profaning the covenant, and the whole is bounded by how God deals with us — not after our sins, but bountifully. A people dealt with on that principle and refusing to deal so with others has misunderstood the mercy it claims.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew gamal (to deal out, to recompense) gives Psalm 13:6 its bounty; bagad (to act treacherously) gives Malachi 2:10 its charge; Greek merizo (to divide, apportion) carries the distributive sense.

expand to see more

Hebrew gamal (H1580) — to deal out, to recompense, to wean; the verb behind “he hath dealt bountifully with me”.

Hebrew bagad (H898) — to act treacherously, to deal falsely; the repeated charge of Malachi 2.

Hebrew parac (H6536) — to break in pieces, to break bread; the breaking implied in dealing bread to the hungry.

Greek merizo (G3307) — to divide, to distribute in portions; the New Testament counterpart of the distributive sense.

Greek koinoneo (G2841) — to share, to communicate; the apostolic word for the same duty of distribution.

Usage

"“Deal thy bread to the hungry” — the bread is the giver's own and the giving is personal."

"“Why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother?” — treachery among brethren profanes the covenant."

"“He hath not dealt with us after our sins” — God's dealing is the measure of ours."
